extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants evaluating U.S. §101 eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (Alice/Mayo framework) to determine whether claims are patent eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101 by (1) identifying statutory category, (2) determining whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, mathematical concept, method of organizing human activity), and (3) assessing whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category check (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites a statutory category of invention (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1: YES if the claim is directed to a statutory category (examples: method/process claims, systems/machines, non-transitory computer-readable media as a manufacture). The examples treat method, system, and non-transitory medium claims as satisfying Step 1 when properly characterized (e.g., a non-transitory computer-readable medium is a manufacture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exception identification (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception such as an abstract idea, mathematical relationship, or method of organizing human activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the claimed subject matter recites concepts similar to those courts have found abstract (e.g., fundamental economic practices, methods of organizing human activity, mathematical relationships, an idea itself). If the claim is directed to such a judicial exception, proceed to Step 2B. If the examiner does not identify an abstract idea recited in the claim, the claim should be deemed not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea subcategories / examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize common categories of judicial exceptions: mathematical operations, fundamental economic practices, organizing human activity, and ideas themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factual analogies: mathematical relationships often fall into the abstract-idea category (e.g., generating a blue noise mask); business arrangements or contractual/financial practices are fundamental economic practices (e.g., transaction guaranty); organizing/management of human activity (e.g., managing Bingo) is another category. Use pertinent Federal Circuit examples to classify the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significantly more / inventive concept (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether additional claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, amount to significantly more than the exception (i.e., provide an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether limitations add meaningful practical application beyond the abstract idea. Generic computer implementation typically does not supply 'significantly more.' However, limitations that improve computer functionality or another technological field (e.g., improved memory use, faster computation, improved signal acquisition) can supply significantly more. Consider both individual elements and their ordered combination (examples: RCT blue-noise mask, SiRF GPS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitations of generic computer components (CPU, memory, display, network, program) performing conventional functions do not by themselves transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computer components are recited at a high level of generality and only perform basic functions (storing, retrieving, transmitting, displaying), treat them as insufficient to supply an inventive concept. Examples: claims that merely say 'perform on a computer' or claim CPU/memory/network to do conventional tasks (Planet Bingo, buySAFE, Ultramercial) are ineligible under Step 2B: NO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer/other technology counts as 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that show an improvement in the functioning of the computer itself or an improvement in another technology/technical field can amount to significantly more than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings of eligibility can rest on showing that the claimed elements yield technological improvements (e.g., reduced memory use, faster computation, improved image quality, enhanced GPS signal-acquisition sensitivity). Use technical fact patterns (blue noise mask halftoning, GPS pseudo-range/server model) to show how the claim improves computer/technical functioning and thus satisfies Step 2B: YES.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rooted in computer technology / internet-centric problem
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed solution that is necessarily rooted in computer technology to solve a problem specifically arising in the realm of computer networks may not be an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish claims that merely apply a business practice on the Internet from those that solve an Internet-specific technical problem (DDR Holdings example). If the claim's limitations are necessarily rooted in computer/internet technology rather than merely implementing a known human/business practice electronically, that favors eligibility (Step 2A: NO or Step 2B: YES depending on context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant pre-solution activity / data-gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities that are mere data gathering or routine, conventional pre-solution steps (e.g., accessing/updating logs, requiring a user's request) are insignificant and do not add 'significantly more'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat steps that merely collect, record, or update information as not contributing an inventive concept (Ultramercial's activity log, consumer request steps). Such steps are considered 'insignificant pre-solution activity' and do not render an abstract idea patent eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered-combination analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess claim elements both individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they together confer significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individual additional elements are generic or insignificant, their particular arrangement or interplay may provide an inventive concept. Examples (RCT, SiRF) analyze the combination of steps/elements and conclude the ordered combination yields improvements that qualify as 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims analyzed under broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation during examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation to claim language when identifying whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception and when evaluating additional limitations. This affects whether features are considered generic or specific enough to supply 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular technological environment is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely stating 'apply the abstract idea on the Internet' or otherwise limiting the idea to a technological environment does not by itself make the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court cautions: 'not all claims purporting to address Internet-centric challenges are eligible'—merely implementing an abstract idea in a particular environment is insufficient; additional meaningful limitations showing technical improvement are required (see DDR cautionary language and Ultramercial reasoning).
